analytic.title: Cache-Aware Task Partitioning for Multicore Real-Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The correct functioning of real-time systems depends not only on the logically correct response, but also the time when it is given. This type of application is increasingly present today and the processing demand is such that complex multi-core processors are needed. The development of multiprocessor is ahead of the techniques of analysis of such systems and it is therefore necessary further research to promote reliability and to reduce over-specified systems. In modern processors, task preemption introduces indirect cost related to the cache memory. A preemption evicts a large amount of memory blocks from the cache memory during the preempting time interval. In this paper we present a partitioning heuristic that includes the cache related preemption delay assumptions in a multiprocessor system with cache memory focusing in partitioned fixed priority preemptive scheduling.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time computer systems are identified as those subjected to temporal requirements [1]. In these systems, the results should be correct not only from the logical perspective, but they also must be generated at the correct time. A timing fault in these systems has sometimes critical consequences. According to [1], real-time systems are classified according to the criticality of their timing requirements. In safety critical real-time systems (hard real-time), the missing of a timing requirement may result in catastrophic consequences both in the economic sense and in human lives. When the timing requirements are not critical (soft real-time), they only describe the desired behavior without resulting in catastrophic consequences.

There are two main approaches to real-time scheduling for multiprocessor: global and partitioned scheduling [2]. In global scheduling, a single scheduler executes tasks by using a global queue and tasks can run on any processor. Furthermore, it allows task preemption and migration. In partitioned scheduling, tasks are statically assigned to a processor and each processor has a task queue and its own scheduler. There are also hybrid solutions that combine global and partitioned scheduling as [3] and [4].

In this paper we will focus on partitioned fixed priority preemptive scheduling. The partitioned scheduling is generally supported by most commercial real-time operating systems [5], besides it is predictable, simple and efficient. Partitioned scheduling can use various well-known monoprocessor real-time scheduling algorithms. However, partitioning is analogous to the bin-packing problem and it is NP-hard in the strong sense. To use the multiprocessor processing power, the scheduling algorithms should work together with the partitioning algorithm. There are numerous task partitioning heuristic and they usually have the following pattern: tasks are sorted under some criteria and they are assigned, in order, to processors. Such bin-packing heuristics are known as First-Fit, Best-Fit, Worst-Fit, among others [6]. However, most scheduling and partition algorithms ignore preemption overheads, especially those related to the cache memory.

In modern processors, task preemption introduces indirect cost related to the cache memory. A preemption evicts a large amount of memory blocks from the cache memory during the preempting time interval (from the preempting instant until resuming the execution). The memory block eviction occurs because other tasks use the cache memory on addition to the system scheduler and others kernel activities. When the preempted task resumes its execution, it requires an amount of time to reload the memory blocks that were previously cached. This memory reloading time increases the execution time of the task, which may invalidate the result of schedulability analysis previously performed, if this effect is not considered in the analysis. This problem is known as cache related preemption delay. Figure 1 shows an example of the cache related preemption delay. Task τ 2 is preempted at time p 2 and when it resumes its execution, a time t c2 is required to reload the cache data. The cache related preemption delay directly affects the response time of task τ 2 , but it also delays the response time of task τ 3 . Task τ 3 should begin at time t i3 and finish at time t ra3 .

In this paper we present a partitioning heuristic that includes the cache related preemption delay assumptions in a multiprocessor system with cache memory. The objective of the algorithm is to assign tasks to a best suited processor in terms of processing capacity and thus, decrease the number of processors needed to schedule the system. In general, previously studies that consider the cache are concerned with data share affinity among tasks and also the size of their Working Set Size, as the work of [7], [8] and [9]. In our work we are concerned about the proper relationship between the scheduling algorithm and the partitioning algorithm when we include the cache related preemption delay in the model.

Section II lists the related work. The task model is described in Section III. In Section IV, we describe the Cache Aware Partition Algorithm. In Section V, the performance of the proposed approach is evaluated and conclusions are presented in Section VI.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: There are several studies in the literature that deal with task allocation in the context of real-time systems due to the significant interest in multicore architectures. There is also significant interest in analyzes that consider the cache related preemption delay since the cache is needed to increase the processor performance.

The work of Oh and Son [10] is one of the first that comes to the partitioning of periodic tasks with fixed priority. They used the First-Fit bin-packing heuristic in conjunction with a utilization based schedulability test. Tasks are sorted by its utilization (U i = Ci Ti ) before the processor allocation. Later, in [11], they present a partitioning algorithm known as first-fit decreasing (FFD) algorithm to a set of sporadic tasks on multiprocessors. Tasks are sorted in non-decreasing relative deadline and they are allocated according to the First-Fit heuristic. In both studies, however, the cache related preemption delay is assumed to be zero or incorporated somehow into the worst case execution time time (WCET) of the task. Thus, the cache related delay is not considered neither in the schedulability test nor during task partitioning.

In [12], it is presented an overview of the impact of the initial task sorting in partitioning periodic tasks scheduled by Rate-Monotonic Priority Ordering. They show that the performance of the heuristics can be improved considering a more appropriate task sorting before partitioning. In [13], it is considered the partitioning of real-time systems with shared resources on multiprocessors. They propose the Blocking-Aware Partitioning Algorithm which aims to reduce the blocking time of the tasks that have shared resources. By reducing task blocking time, in general, it could increase the schedulability and thus reduce the number of processors required to schedule the system. The partitioning solution of [13] considers shared resources but in a way that is similar to our concern about the cache related preemption delay.

Since we are focusing on multiprocessor tasks partitioning with fixed priority and cache related preemption delay, it is interesting to describe some works related to schedulability analysis. In [14], it is described one of the first works that extended the response time schedulability test to incorporate the cache related preemption delay. They incorporate the cache related preemption delay into the response time analysis equation. However, this preliminary work focused on the introduction of the schedulability test, but not how to calculate the cache preemption delay. Later in [15] and [16], the cache related preemption delay schedulability analysis is reformulated as an optimization problem.

Several studies including [17] shows how to calculate the preemption delay as a task parameter (numerical value) to use in the response time analysis. This work reintroduced the concept of useful cache blocks (UCB) and evicted cache blocks (ECB) and they described a new approach known as ECB-Union. As described by Lee et al. [15], a useful cache block is a block that is cached at some program point and it will be reused later in another reachable program point. The task preemption cost is calculated at the program point with the highest number of useful cache blocks. An evicted cache block is a memory block accessed during the execution of the preempting tasks. The worst-case cost of a preemption is the number of cache blocks that the task may evict during this execution. If we use both concepts, UCB and ECB, a tighter cache related preemption delay can be calculated because we know which blocks are useful at every task program point and we know exactly which cache blocks will be evicted by preempting tasks. Therefore, the approach described in [17] is less pessimistic because it considers the cache memory interaction between tasks, ie only cache blocks that would be effectively evicted during a preemption are considered in the preemption cost. As pointed out by [17] and [15], we can calculate the cache preemption delay as an individual parameter of each task to finally consider it in the schedulability analysis. In this paper we assume task execution independence, which means that we can't use any ECB approach. In order to use an ECB approach to calculate the cache preemption delay we have to know all preempting tasks during a task execution and we don't know this before the task partitioning. So, in this paper, cache related preemption delay could be calculated using the UCB approach.

div.head: III. TASK MODEL
div.p: In this paper we assume a sporadic task model where a sporadic task τ i = (C i , D i , T i , γ i ) is characterized by its worst case execution time (WCET) C i , its deadline D i , its minimum interval between arrivals or period T i and a penalty γ i related to preemption. The term γ is associated with the preemptive scheduling strategy and corresponds to a time to recharge cache memory. C i corresponds to the WCET without preemption, while the WCET increases by the γ penalty in case of a preemptive scheme. γ can be evaluated using the useful cache block (UCB) approach [15].

Each task τ i generates an infinite sequence of jobs. Each job has worst case execution time C i . A job of τ i that is ready for execution at time t has an absolute deadline t+D i and the generation of successive instances are separated by at least T i units of time.

It is assumed that the system consists of a set Π of m identical processors where Π = {π 1 , π 2 ...π m }, and a set of tasks T . Let T be formed by n independent sporadic tasks where T = {τ 1 , τ 2 , τ i , ..., τ n } and τ i = (C i , D i , T i , γ i ) for all i, with 1 ≤ i ≤ n. A task τ i ∈ T πj represents a task τ i running on processor π j , ie T πj corresponds to a set of tasks running on processor j, with 1 ≤ j ≤ m. Furthermore it is assumed that the relative deadlines satisfy the condition

This task model does not allow migration of tasks and the system belongs to the class of partitioned scheduling. In this context, the set of tasks T is partitioned into a number of disjoint subsets, and each subset is associated with a single processor (π 1 , π 2 , ...π m ). All instances generated by a task must run in its corresponding processor. Figure 2 shows the system processor-memory hierarchy. We assume that all π processors have their own disjoint level 1 cache memory (one date cache memory and one instruction cache memory). A Random Access Memory is above the level 1 cache and there is no shared cache between the processors. Disjoint caches and simple memory architectures are important to make the hardware timing predictable as described in [18].

div.head: IV. THE CACHE AWARE PARTITION ALGORITHM
div.p: In this section we describe our partitioning algorithm that considers the cache related preemption delay during task partitioning. Fundamentally, task partitioning is usually solved by bin-packing heuristic, which have the following pattern:
• tasks are sorted by some criteria;
• tasks of the sorted list are assigned, in order, to a processor;

• in each task assignment, task set schedulability is checked by executing a monoprocessor schedulability analysis; • after task assignment, if any task belonging to that processor is not schedulable, another processor is chosen to execute the last assigned task. The first step in the development of the Cache Aware Partition Algorithm was choosing the task sorting criteria. The partitioning success is sorting sensitive [12]. We must choose a function that transmits the task size in the best possible way. Typically, in fixed priority scheduling, sorting by non-increasing utilization (U i = Ci Ti ) has the best results. However, this is not true when we are considering the cache related preemption delay. The partitioning sensitivity with respect to the sorting criteria is also verified by [13]. They introduce a new task weight function when tasks have shared resources, ie tasks are not independent.
In the case of the Cache Aware Partition Algorithm, we use the U * function described by Equation 1 as task sorting criteria. Tasks are sorted by non-increasing

div.p: The basic idea behind U * i sorting is to first assign heavier tasks, considering both its computation time C i and its amount of cache related preemption delay γ i . Several binpacking studies show that assigning first heavier elements to bins improves the overall result of the allocation [6][13], ie fewer processors are needed.

The second step in the development of Cache Aware Partition Algorithm was to determine the monoprocessor schedulability test. In our approach, we used the response time test proposed by [14] according to Equation 2. Equation 2 is also used in [17]. The test calculates the task worst case response time considering the critical instant, the interference of all higher priority tasks and the cache related preemption delay using a fixed point equation. The preemption delay γ i appears as an interference summed to the computation time of all higher priority tasks (j ∈ hp(i)). The γ i can be calculated using the Useful Cache Block (UCB) approach [15].

Finally, we must choose which processor a task will be assigned during partitioning. We use the Best-Fit heuristic, where we maintain a sorted list of processors ordered by non-increasing total utilization plus γ defined by Equation 3. The first processor chosen during allocation is the processor with high capacity already allocated. If the task to be allocated does not fit, we try the second processor and so on until the task is allocated or a new empty processor is used.

div.head: V. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION AND COMPARISON OF ALGORITHMS
div.p: In this section we evaluate the performance of the Cache Aware Partition Algorithm comparing it with the classic approach DMBFDU (Deadline Monotonic Best Fit Decreasing Utilization). DMBFDU uses utilization (U i = Ci Ti ) as sorting criteria, but for the schedulability test we use Equation 2to consider the cache related preemption delay effect. The empirical evaluation considers the following randomly generated parameters: • minimum arrival intervals (T i ) were generated according to a uniform distribution with a logarithmic factor of 1000 between the minimum and maximum values of 1ms to 1 second. The logarithmic uniform distribution was used because it generates an equal number of tasks in each logarithmic time interval (1-10ms, 100ms, etc.); • worst-case computation time based on its utilization:
div.formula: C i = U i * T i ; • constrained task deadlines: D i ≤ T i ;
div.p: • Deadline Monotonic priority assignment. The cache related preemption delay (γ) was also randomly generated as described in [17], however:
• cache size was increased to 1024 sets;

• cache utilization of each task was generated using the UUnifast Algorithm [19], but total cache utilization of the task set CU varies as follows CU = sys_U * n_tasks/4. sys U is the task set total utilization ([0.1 , 4] and [0.4, 8] with 40 checkpoints per interval) and n_tasks is the number of the task in the task set (20 and 40 tasks).

We defined CU formulation empirically as we cannot make an exhaustive evaluation of all parameters, but it uses the following logic. In [17], they use initially CU = 10 for all task sets. However, in our work, the cache utilization should vary somehow as the system utilization and the task number increase. CU = sys_U * n_tasks/4 is a weighing cache utilization variation where one task set with lower utilization should use less cache than one with higher utilization. If we pin CU in a very high value for all utilization interval, task sets with low utilization will be severally penalized while task sets with higher utilization will not.

We present two test conditions: 4 processors with 20 tasks and 16 processors with 80 tasks. In each one, we are interested in the percentage of systems that are effectively schedulable at each utilization level. Figures 3 and4 present the results for both conditions. In these figures, we present three performance curves: performance of the DMBFDU (Deadline Monotonic Best Fit Decreasing Utilization) without considering the preemption cost ("No Preemption Cost" label), Classic Partitioning using DMBFDU considering the preemption cost and the Cache Aware Partition Algorithm performance. We present the DMBFDU curve without considering the preemption cost just to illustrate an scheduling upper bound of the task set. We are not interested in scheduling without taking into account the cache related preemption delay.

We can see that our algorithm outperforms the classic partitioning of DMBFDU in both scenarios. Obviously, an exhaustive evaluation of all parameters combination is not possible, but based on our tests (not only the two presented in this paper), we can see a significant schedulability gain when we consider the cache related preemption delay during task partitioning. We have evaluated our algorithm using others scenarios like 32 processors and 160 tasks but those graphs are omitted because they deliver same conclusions. In fact, the correct sorting of task and processors during the partitioning is crucial in terms of performance.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper we presented a partitioning heuristic that considers the cache related preemption delay. It is an extension of the bin packing problem facing the task partitioning in real-time systems that distribute tasks among unity capacity identical processors.

The main contribution of this paper is to introduce a better function responsible for task and processor sorting that generates the Cache Aware Partition Algorithm. This algorithm allocates first heavier tasks considering both task individual utilization and task individual preemption cost. We show that using the Cache Aware Partitioning Algorithm there is schedulability improvement.

The Cache Aware Partition Algorithm was developed considering partitioned systems with fixed priority because many practical real-time systems use fixed priority scheduling. Any priority policy can be used. Moreover, partitioned systems are characterized by predictability, simplicity and efficiency, and we can extend the partitioning algorithm to include any monoprocessor schedulability test.

Experiments showed that our algorithm has superior performance compared to existing heuristics. We do not know any partitioning algorithm that considers the cache related preemption delay as it was showed here. However, we must remember that partitioning is NP-Hard, and so we did not obtain an optimal solution.

In future works, we will evaluate the algorithm performance using other scheduling policies. An interesting aspect is to investigate additional functions to improve the cache preemption delay capture in different situations, considering, for example, different cache architectures. One of the first future extension of the Cache Aware Partition Algorithm is to use more precise cache preemption calculation methods, for example, ECB (Evicted Cache Blocks) approaches. Using the ECB techniques we have do discard the task independence assumption and reformulate the Cache Aware Partition Algorithm.
